opus-5.5.text:
I think humanoids are really exciting, and there's a lot of appeal to the idea that the world is built for humans, so a robot shaped like a human should be able to operate in it. But when I think about it from the perspective of data, which I think is really the main bottleneck right now, I'm a bit more cautious.

One of the hardest parts of getting a humanoid to work is just collecting high-quality demonstration data. Teleoperating a humanoid with lots of degrees of freedom, including legs, balance, two arms, and dexterous hands, is quite hard. The operator has to control a lot at once, and if the robot falls over, that's costly and slows everything down. With a simpler platform, say a pair of arms on a stable base, or even a mobile manipulator with wheels, you can collect a lot more data, a lot faster, and with fewer failures. Data collection throughput really matters when you're trying to train general-purpose models.

I also don't think you need legs for a huge fraction of the useful tasks people care about. Many tasks in homes, warehouses, and kitchens can be done with wheels and a couple of arms. So in the near term, I'd lean toward form factors that are cheaper, more reliable, and easier to collect data on.

That said, I'm not against humanoids at all. One thing we've seen is that training across many different robot embodiments actually helps. Data from one robot can transfer to another. So I think the right approach is to build models that can control many types of robots, humanoids included, rather than betting everything on one form factor. As the models get better and need less data per robot, the hardware question becomes less of a bottleneck, and humanoids may make a lot more sense. Right now, though, I think the focus should be on getting the intelligence right, and on platforms where you can iterate quickly.

r001.rationale: It says humanoids are hard to teleoperate because they have many degrees of freedom, and contrasts them with stable-base or wheeled platforms that are easier to operate and collect data with.

r002.rationale: It recommends near-term platforms that are cheaper, more reliable, and easier to collect data on, explicitly tying platform choice to data-collection throughput.

r003.rationale: It says better models may need less data per robot and make hardware less of a bottleneck, but does not clearly state that obtaining abundant training data would shift progress constraints away from data availability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that humanoids are a bet, and it's worth being clear about what the bet actually is. The argument for the form factor is that the world is built for humans. Doorways, stairs, kitchen counters, tools, all of it is designed around a body like ours. So if you can get a humanoid to work, you don't have to redesign the environment, and that's a big deal if your goal is general-purpose robots in homes and workplaces.

But from the data perspective, which is really the thing I care most about, the picture is more mixed. On one hand, a humanoid is appealing because there's this hope that you can leverage human video, people doing tasks in the world, and there's a lot of that. The morphology matches, so in principle the transfer should be easier than mapping a human arm onto a two-fingered gripper on a wheeled base. On the other hand, in practice that transfer is still really hard. Human video doesn't give you the actions, it doesn't give you the forces, the contact, the joint torques. So you still need real robot data, and humanoids are expensive, fragile, and hard to teleoperate well. Collecting high-quality demonstrations on a bipedal robot with dexterous hands is just a harder operational problem than collecting data on a stable arm on a table.

The thing I keep coming back to is that the bottleneck for robot learning right now isn't really the hardware, it's the data and the generality of the models. And we've seen with things like the cross-embodiment work that you can train on data from lots of different robots and get positive transfer. So I don't think you need to commit to one form factor to make progress on the foundation model side. You can collect on whatever platforms are cheapest and most reliable today, and let the model absorb that, and then the humanoid becomes one more embodiment you fine-tune into rather than the thing you have to bootstrap from scratch.

So my assessment is that humanoids are probably the right long-term target for a lot of applications, but if you optimize purely for learning as fast as possible right now, they're not obviously the best vehicle for data collection. I'd rather have a huge amount of diverse, messy data across simpler robots than a small amount of pristine data on a humanoid. And I think the groups that will do well are the ones that treat the form factor as a downstream question and the data and the model as the upstream one.

r001.rationale: It says collecting demonstrations on a bipedal humanoid is harder than on a stable arm on a table, a static manipulator.

r002.rationale: It recommends collecting data on platforms that are cheapest and most reliable, and describes simpler robots as better for learning quickly now.

r003.rationale: It identifies data as a current bottleneck and advocates collecting more diverse data, but does not say abundant data would shift constraints away from data availability.

astra-6.text:
I think humanoids are a compelling form factor because so much of our world is designed around the human body. But from a data collection perspective, the form factor alone doesn’t solve the problem. You still need a way to get the robot to perform useful behaviors and collect enough varied experience for it to generalize.

There’s an appealing argument that, because a humanoid looks like a person, it should be able to learn directly from videos of people. And human video can certainly provide information about tasks and how objects behave. But it doesn’t tell you exactly what forces to apply or what actions will work on a particular robot. There’s still a gap between observing a person do something and being able to execute it reliably.

So I’d think about the body and the data collection strategy together. Can you teleoperate it effectively? Can it collect experience safely and consistently? And do you actually need legs for the tasks you’re trying to learn? For some applications, a mobile robot with arms might let you collect useful data much more easily. Humanoids could be very versatile, but I wouldn’t assume they’re automatically the best starting point.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a humanoid can be teleoperated effectively, but does not say humanoids are harder to teleoperate than static or wheeled manipulators.

r002.rationale: It says to consider the body and data collection strategy together, asking whether the platform can collect experience safely and consistently and noting that a mobile robot with arms may make data collection easier.

r003.rationale: It discusses the need for enough varied experience, but does not state that abundant robot data would shift progress constraints away from data availability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think humanoids are a really interesting form factor, but they don’t automatically solve the data problem. There’s this appealing argument that the world is built for humans, so if you build a robot that looks like a human, you can learn from all this data of people doing things. And I think there’s something to that. Human video can tell you a lot about what tasks look like and how objects interact. But it doesn’t directly tell you what actions the robot should take, what forces it should apply, or how to recover when something goes wrong.

You still need data from the robot itself. And there, a humanoid introduces some challenges: it’s a more complex system, it can fall over, and collecting data reliably can be harder than with a stationary arm or a wheeled robot.

So I’m excited about humanoids, especially for tasks where you really need to operate in human environments. But I wouldn’t assume that matching the human body is necessarily the fastest path to collecting useful training data. I’d ask what tasks you want the robot to do, and then what hardware lets you collect lots of diverse experience safely and reliably.

r001.rationale: The response says humanoids can be harder for reliable data collection than stationary arms or wheeled robots, but it does not state that they are harder to teleoperate.

r002.rationale: It recommends choosing hardware that enables lots of diverse experience to be collected safely and reliably.

r003.rationale: It does not say abundant robot training data would shift progress constraints away from data availability; it says robot-specific data is still needed.
